claims.text: The target components are high-value steel parts with localized surface damage.
The target steel microstructure is prone to hot cracking during fusion-welding repair.
Alloy powders can be spark-plasma-sintered to produce electrodes suitable for electrospark deposition.
Multilayer electrospark deposition using those electrodes will form a protective surface cladding.
The deposited multilayer cladding will have a refined, alloyed microstructure.
The cladding will have superior grain-boundary integrity and metallurgical bonding at the substrate interface.
The cladding structure and bonding will reduce internal stresses and minimize defects.
The rapid, localized energy input of electrospark deposition preserves a fine-grained microstructure.
Electrospark deposition effectively distributes alloying elements within the cladding.
The fine-grained, compositionally distributed cladding limits crack initiation and propagation during service.
Traditional fusion-welding repair creates a more extensive heat-affected zone than electrospark deposition.
Traditional fusion-welded repairs have a higher propensity for hot cracking.
The electrospark-deposited cladding will minimize hot-cracking risk relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
The cladded surface will have approximately 20–30% greater hardness than fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The cladded surface will have approximately 15–25% lower corrosion rate than fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The cladded surface will have approximately 15–25% lower wear rate than fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
The intervention is expected to be most effective for compatible steel chemistries with moderate surface damage.
Extreme substrate-alloy variation or substantially different damage mechanisms may limit performance.
Performance depends on alloy composition, deposition parameters, and scale-up from laboratory to industrial conditions.
Failure to exceed the fusion-welded repair by at least 10% in hardness and corrosion resistance, or observation of similar or higher crack density, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
